content: Students may find value in collaborative peer assessment methods, as these approaches enable them to work together on case studies in real time. This collaboration not only enhances their learning experience but also fosters the formation of social connections and a sense of belonging, particularly during clinical assignments. Key features of mobile learning (mLearning) programs that students appreciate include the rapid retrieval of reference materials, the ability to quickly store resources such as text and images for future use, and the option to customize the learning content or program layout to meet their individual needs. Many students prefer mLearning over traditional textbooks, as mobile devices are portable and allow them to utilize small blocks of time, such as waiting between patient consultations or for senior staff, for learning activities. Despite the associated costs, some students prefer using their own devices, as this allows them to engage with technology informally and at times that suit their schedules. However, there are factors that may reduce the acceptability of mLearning. Some students and tutors note that while digital devices can enhance communication between clinicians and patients, they may also negatively impact patient interactions. For example, devices might interfere with bedside activities, such as medical consultations, clinical observations, and teamwork. Using devices in front of patients may be perceived as rude or awkward, and some students may feel uncomfortable due to a lack of technological skills. Additionally, the inability to maintain good eye contact with patients while using devices can hinder effective communication. Students may also worry about being perceived as unprofessional by patients or colleagues, who might associate device use with leisure rather than learning. Supervising staff in clinical settings may disapprove of device use, leading students to hesitate in using them openly. Concerns also exist regarding the content provided through mLearning apps or websites. Both students and tutors may question the trustworthiness or reliability of the information, as well as its timing and alignment with the rest of the curriculum or clinical practice. Some students and lecturers express frustration with the learning curve associated with using new devices. Even technologically proficient students report needing support and repeated training to become familiar with devices, although comfort with mobile devices tends to improve over time. Clinical instructors may also lack sufficient knowledge of these devices, further complicating their integration into learning activities. Additionally, some students report being too busy to incorporate devices into their practice or are reluctant to invest time in integrating them into their daily routines. Limited guidance on how to effectively use mobile devices for learning further exacerbates this issue. Some students may prefer traditional learning methods, such as paper-based materials and face-to-face communication, over mLearning approaches. There is also concern about over-reliance on devices, particularly regarding potential technology failures or the impact on recall abilities during exams. Systematic reviews of global evidence highlight several challenges to the feasibility of digital health interventions, including issues with network connectivity, access to electricity, system integration, device usability, and health worker training. These challenges are particularly pronounced in rural or peripheral settings, where health workers may face geographic barriers, poor network coverage, limited access to electricity, lower levels of digital literacy, and fewer resources, including smartphones. The implementation of mLearning programs requires significant resources. One-time start-up costs include the adaptation of training content into digital formats, such as videos and multimedia, which may involve translating content into different languages or skill levels. Technology adaptation costs include software customization to integrate training content, user testing to ensure optimal user experience, and refinement based on feedback. Initial training for health workers interacting with the system is also necessary, as is refresher training to maintain proficiency. Communication and data exchange costs may arise if training content is not stored on devices, and ongoing technology maintenance costs include software updates, hardware insurance, and replacement. These resource considerations assume the availability of electricity, network connectivity, and pre-registration training for health workers, as well as their availability and remuneration for providing health services.
